rv.q: With its uniformly good cast, tight direction and frequent flashes of humor, Lombardi is solid playing in every sense of the word.
Mr. Lauria knows a dream part when he sees one, and makes the most of this one.

Light is stunning as his wife, a woman who reluctantly left her life in New Jersey for Wisconsin's frozen tundra. She wears a helmet of '60s-housewife hair, likes downing highballs and has some of the driest, funniest lines. The visiting journalist soon recognizes that she's the key person to talk to, much as she is the fulcrum of the play.
While Simonson’s play is very effective when it’s focused on the Lombardis’ marriage, it falters on other counts.
Dan Lauria brings gruff authority and unexpected warmth to his portrayal of the legendary Green Bay Packers coach in this workmanlike biographical drama.
The show looks back in wonder at the famed Green Bay Packers coach, but curiously lacks momentum.
But it is entertaining and there’s a place for it in the Broadway huddle.
It’s hard to believe that in 2010 we can still romanticize selfish, abusive bastards, even if they’re gifted enough to turn a losing team into winners.
Although we are dutifully fed plenty of information about Lombardi’s life and career, Simonson has failed to construct interesting drama out of it.

For someone not previously enthralled with Vince Lombardi's famous winning streak as coach of the Green Bay Packers in the '60s, the only compelling part of Eric Simonson's untheatrical script is the mystery of what it's doing on Broadway.
What no actor could provide is the compelling emotional or psychological substance that’s absent from the writing.
Even if you never cared about Lombardi, you’ll enjoy “Lombardi.” And that really is everything.

If you know who Vince Lombardi is, the play is most likely exactly what you'd expect it to be: a portrait of decent, honorable figure who earns the devotion of his players by tough-loving them into the best they're capable of being.
Of course, Lombardi is not a show to diminish its hero, and with Lauria and Light's sterling duet, fans can rest assured that their champion's legacy is secure.
And while he's blessed with a solid team, 'Lombardi' the play isn't entirely a winner.
Lombardi may aspire to and achieve something less, but there are worse ways to spend 95 minutes.
“Lombardi” never quite achieves the greatness of the coach’s briefly invincible team.
Produced in league with the NFL, “Lombardi” is more like a 90-minute tribute than a full-contact drama.
"Lombardi" may bring a whole new audience of sports fans to Broadway, but theater fans will recognize it as an incomplete pass.

Eric Simonson's play is told through the eyes of a Look magazine reporter who spent a week with Lombardi during the 1965 season, providing an excuse for lots of irrelevant talk about editors and deadlines, but almost no useful insights into Lombardi (played, just adequately, by former Wonder Years star Dan Lauria), aside from the fact that he ap...
I thoroughly enjoyed this production, and credit the stellar performances of this ensemble cast.
The acting is brilliant, the story's compelling and there are genuine moments of triumph, tension and despair.

Producers of "Lombardi" have been shrewd. They’ve seemingly come across theatrical catnip for husbands or boyfriends otherwise reluctant to see most Broadway shows: Football! Vince Lombardi! The legendary Packers!
Football fans lured by the subject to a Broadway show probably can overlook the gaps in Simonson's solid if mechanical drama.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actress in a Play

cn.t: Critics find this Vince Lombardi bio-drama workmanlike but uninspired, praising Dan Lauria's gruff performance and Judith Light's work as his wife while faulting the conventional structure and lack of deeper insight into the legendary coach.
